LocaleContent.title: Step 1
LocaleContent.content:
Access Server Manager and Configure System Time

In this section, you will utilize Server Manager to navigate to the Local Server view and manually adjust the system's date and time settings to match a known good source (your laptop). Server Manager is the primary administrative tool for Windows Server, allowing you to monitor and configure current system states.

Configuring accurate time is critical for a Data Systems Administrator. It ensures proper authentication, accurate system logging, and reliable synchronization with other systems. If the time is incorrect, systems may fail to trust each other, which can disrupt domain communications, network operations, and ultimately mission systems.

Step Action & Verification
1 Open Server Manager and select the Local Server view from the left pane to review the current configuration and status of the server.
2 In the Properties tile, click on the hyperlinked time next to Time zone to open the system date and time settings.
3 Click the Change date and time... button to open the menu that allows for manual adjustments.
4 Adjust the server’s date, time, and AM/PM settings so that they match your laptop.
5 Click OK to apply the changes.
6 Verification: Confirm the updated time is now correctly reflected in the Local Server properties dashboard.

LocaleContent.title: Set Correct Date and Time
LocaleContent.content:
All the following steps will be conducted on the virtual machine labeled NDSACDC01 in your console menu.

Target VM Credentials

  • Target System: NDSACDC01
  • Username: xadministrator
  • Password: M@rines1M@rines1

LocaleContent.title: Step 1
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are opening the Local Group Policy Editor by typing gpedit.msc.

Why this matters:
Group Policy controls security and system behavior on Windows servers. As a data systems administrator, you must know how to access this tool to configure security settings such as the firewall

​​​​​​​Click the windows key and type gpedit.msc ​​​​​​​and open the group policy editor.

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 2
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are expanding Computer Configuration and then Windows Settings within the Group Policy Editor.

Why this matters:
System‑wide security settings are organized under Computer Configuration. Knowing how to navigate this structure allows you to locate and adjust critical security controls

​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 3
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are expanding Security Settings, then Windows Defender Firewall, and selecting the Windows Defender Firewall option.

Why this matters:
This location contains the firewall policies that control how the server allows or blocks network traffic. Accessing this area is required before making any firewall changes

​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 4
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are selecting Windows Defender Firewall Properties.

Why this matters:
Firewall Properties allow you to configure firewall behavior for different network profiles (Domain, Private, and Public), which directly affects server connectivity

LocaleContent.title: Step 5
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are setting the Firewall state to Off for the Domain Profile.

Why this matters:
In a training environment, disabling the firewall prevents it from blocking required services during server setup and configuration

LocaleContent.title: Step 6
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are repeating the same firewall setting change for the Private Profile.

Why this matters:
Ensuring the firewall is disabled across profiles prevents connectivity issues if the server identifies the network as private

LocaleContent.title: Step 7
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are disabling the firewall under the Public Profile as well.

Why this matters:
This ensures the firewall does not interfere with network communication during the lab, even if the network type changes

LocaleContent.title: Step 8
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are clicking OK to save the firewall settings and returning to Server Manager.

Why this matters:
Firewall changes do not take effect until they are confirmed. Returning to Server Manager allows you to continue configuring the server

LocaleContent.title: Step 1 v1
LocaleContent.content:
Step 1: Access the Local Group Policy Editor

In this section, you will launch the Local Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc) on the server. Group Policy controls critical security baselines and operating system behavior across Windows Server environments. As a data systems administrator, accessing this tool is a prerequisite for managing administrative templates, user rights, and network security controls such as the Windows Defender Firewall.

Step Action & Verification
1 Click the Windows Key (or open the Start menu).
2 Type gpedit.msc and press Enter to open the Local Group Policy Editor.
3 Verification: Confirm that the Local Group Policy Editor management console opens, displaying the Local Computer Policy tree in the left navigation pane.
4 Remediation (If required): If the Run dialog or Start search fails to locate the file, open an administrative PowerShell prompt, type gpedit.msc, and press Enter.
Console Navigation Reference
Firewall Properties Reference

LocaleContent.title: Step 2 v1
LocaleContent.content:
Step 1: Access the Local Group Policy Editor

In this section, you will launch the Local Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc) on the server. Group Policy controls critical security baselines and operating system behavior across Windows Server environments. As a data systems administrator, you must know how to access and manage this tool to configure essential security settings, including the Windows Defender Firewall.

Step Action & Reference Image
1 Click the Windows Key (or click the Start button) to open the Start menu.
2 Type gpedit.msc into the search bar.
3 Select gpedit.msc from the search results.
4 Click Open (or press Enter) to launch the management console.
Verification: Confirm that the Local Group Policy Editor window opens successfully and displays the Local Computer Policy tree in the left navigation pane.
Remediation (If required): If the Start search does not locate the console, press Windows Key + R to open the Run dialog, enter gpedit.msc, and press Enter.

LocaleContent.title: Disable Firewall
LocaleContent.content:
In this section, you will log into the NDSACDC01 Virtual Machine and utilize the Local Group Policy Editor to disable the Windows Defender Firewall. Disabling the local firewall is often required in closed lab and field environments to ensure unobstructed communication between internal domain services, routing protocols, and administrative management tools without interference during initial configuration.

Target VM Credentials

  • Target System: NDSACDC01

LocaleContent.title: Step 1
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are clicking on the IPv4 address currently assigned to the server from the Local Server view in Server Manager.

Why this matters:
This opens the network configuration for the server. Since the address is currently assigned by DHCP, it must be changed to a static IP that fits the network design

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 2
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are opening the Ethernet network adapter to view its connection details.

Why this matters:
Accessing the Ethernet adapter is required to modify the network protocols and IP configuration used by the server

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 3
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are selecting Properties for the Ethernet adapter.

Why this matters:
The Properties menu allows you to configure which network protocols the adapter uses and how they are configured, including IP addressing

​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 4
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are opening Internet Protocol Version 4 (IPv4) settings.

Why this matters:
IPv4 controls how the server communicates on the network. Proper IPv4 configuration is required for reliable connectivity and service availability

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 5
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are selecting Use the following IP address and Use the following DNS server addresses, then entering the provided network information.

Why this matters:
Assigning a static IP and DNS configuration ensures the server can always be located on the network and can properly resolve names for domain and network services

​​​​​​​

  1. IP Address: 192.168.40.2
  2. Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0
  3. Default gateway: 192.168.40.1
  4. Preferred DNS server: 192.168.40.2
  5. Alternate DNS server: 192.168.40.3​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ ​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 6
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are clicking OK to save the IPv4 configuration.

Why this matters:
Network changes do not take effect until they are applied. Saving these settings ensures the server begins using the new static configuration

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 7
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are closing the Ethernet Properties window by clicking OK.

Why this matters:
Closing the properties confirms that all network changes are finalized and applied to the adapter

​​​​​​​

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Configure network adapter settings
LocaleContent.content: ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​The network IP address for the server has not been set yet and is set to DHCP. You want your servers to be static IP addresses so they never change. ​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 1
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are accessing the system settings where the computer name can be changed.

Why this matters:
This menu allows administrators to modify system‑level identity settings, including the name the server uses to identify itself on the network.

​​​​​​​

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 2
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are clicking Change to open the dialog box that allows you to rename the computer.

Why this matters:
The Change option is required to modify the server’s computer name so it can follow the proper naming convention

​​​​​​​

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 3
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are changing the computer name to NDSACDC01 and clicking OK.

Why this matters:
Using a standardized name helps administrators immediately identify this server as a domain controller. This reduces confusion and supports effective network management

​​​​​​​

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 4
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are acknowledging the notification that changing the computer name requires a restart by clicking OK.

Why this matters:
System‑level changes such as a computer name update do not take effect until the server restarts. Acknowledging this ensures the process can continue correctly​​​​​​​

​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 5
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are restarting the server to apply the new computer name.

Why this matters:
Restarting ensures the new computer name is fully applied and recognized by the operating system and the network before moving on to additional configuration tasks.

​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Step 6
LocaleContent.content:
You will be given the option to restart now or restart later. It is highly recommended to always choose restart now in case you forget to do it later. Click RESTART NOW.

​​​​​​​

LocaleContent.title: Change Computer Name
LocaleContent.content:
​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

What you are doing:
You are renaming the server to a standardized computer name.

Why this matters:
Server names identify the role and purpose of a system on the network. Consistent naming conventions make it easier for administrators to manage, troubleshoot, and identify servers in both garrison and operational environments.

LocaleContent.title: Step 1
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are assigning a different static IP configuration to the secondary domain controller than the one used on the primary domain controller.

Why this matters:
Each server on the network must have a unique IP address. Using the correct addressing scheme prevents network conflicts and ensures both domain controllers can operate simultaneously

Secondary Domain Controller IP Settings:

  • IP address: 192.168.40.3
  • Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0
  • Default gateway: 192.168.40.1
  • Preferred DNS server: 192.168.40.2
  • Alternate DNS server: 192.168.40.3

LocaleContent.title: Step 2
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are assigning a different computer name to the secondary domain controller.

Why this matters:
Each domain controller must have a unique name so administrators can clearly identify its role and distinguish it from the primary domain controller during management and troubleshooting.

Secondary Domain Controller Name:

  • NDSACDC02

LocaleContent.title: Setting up secondary domain controller.
LocaleContent.content:
What you are doing:
You are configuring a secondary domain controller using the same baseline configuration steps as the primary domain controller.

Why this matters:
A secondary domain controller provides redundancy. If the primary domain controller becomes unavailable, authentication and directory services can continue, which is critical for maintaining network operations and mission continuity.

LocaleContent.title: DSAC Annex B | Lab 1: Installing and Configuring Windows Server
LocaleContent.content:
WINDOWS SERVER 2022

Windows Server is the backbone operating system used across Marine Corps enterprise and tactical networks to manage user accounts, control access, and run critical network services. As a Data Systems Administrator, your job is to build and maintain these systems so mission-critical applications stay online and secure. In this lab, you will learn the fundamental skills required to get a server up and running from scratch—including completing the initial operating system installation, navigating Server Manager, setting the system hostname and accurate time, and configuring basic local policies before deploying the server into an operational network.

INSTRUCTIONAL PURPOSE

This annex is developed for instructional use in the United States Marine Corps entry-level school for MOS 0671 – Data Systems Administrator.

It provides a structured, step-by-step approach to installing, configuring, and operating within a Windows Server environment. Students will learn how to complete an initial operating system installation, navigate Server Manager, configure system hostnames and time settings, and perform baseline administrative tasks in support of Marine Corps network environments.
